content.text:
# How Rivers Form

A river looks permanent, but it is really the result of water, gravity, rock and time working together. Every river starts in a small way, and its shape keeps changing over centuries and millennia.

## The Water Cycle as the Engine

Rivers begin with the water cycle. The sun heats oceans, lakes and soil, and water evaporates into the air. As the moist air rises and cools, the vapor condenses into clouds and eventually falls as rain or snow. When that precipitation lands on high ground, gravity starts pulling it downhill toward the sea. That downhill pull is what makes a river possible.

Not all precipitation turns into flowing water at once. Some soaks into the ground and recharges aquifers, some evaporates again, and plants take some up. The rest becomes surface runoff, which runs across the land when the soil is saturated or the rain falls faster than the ground can absorb it.

## Sources and Headwaters

Most rivers start in highlands such as mountains, hills or plateaus, where the land is steep and precipitation is often heavy. The source might be a spring where groundwater comes to the surface, a melting glacier, a mountain lake overflowing its basin, or simply many small trickles of runoff coming together on a slope.

These first flows are tiny. Water collects in small dips and cracks in the land and forms rills, narrow channels only a few centimeters deep. Rills join to form gullies, gullies join to form streams, and streams merge into larger and larger channels. Hydrologists describe this branching pattern with stream order: two first-order streams join to make a second-order stream, two second-order streams make a third-order stream, and so on. The Amazon and the Mississippi are the product of thousands of these joins.

## Carving the Channel

Moving water erodes the land it flows over. It does this in several ways. Hydraulic action is the force of the water itself prying loose sediment and breaking apart weak rock. Abrasion happens when sand, gravel and boulders carried by the current scrape and grind the riverbed like sandpaper. Solution, or corrosion, is the chemical dissolving of soluble rocks such as limestone.

Rivers are steep and fast in their upper reaches, so they cut downward most aggressively there. This vertical erosion creates V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, rapids and gorges. Waterfalls often form where a band of hard rock sits on top of softer rock: the soft rock wears away faster, the hard ledge is undercut, and the falls slowly retreat upstream.

## The Middle and Lower Course

As a river moves away from the mountains, the slope flattens and the river gains volume from its tributaries. Its energy shifts from cutting downward to cutting sideways. The current flows faster on the outside of bends, eroding those banks, and slower on the inside, where sediment drops out. Over time this process creates meanders, the looping curves typical of mature rivers. A meander can eventually loop so far that the river cuts across its neck during a flood and leaves behind a crescent-shaped oxbow lake.

In the lower course, the river spreads across a wide, flat floodplain. During floods it overflows its banks and leaves layers of fertile silt behind, which is why floodplains have supported farming for thousands of years. Repeated flooding can also build natural levees, raised ridges of sediment along the banks.

## Reaching the Sea

Where a river meets the ocean or a lake, it slows sharply and drops the rest of its sediment load. If tides and currents are weak, this sediment builds up into a delta, a fan of land crossed by smaller branching channels, like the Nile or the Mississippi deltas. If tides are strong, the river mouth may instead form an estuary, where fresh water and salt water mix.

## A System Always Changing

A river is never really finished. Tectonic uplift, changing climates, glaciers, landslides and human engineering all keep reshaping its course. Even so, the basic process stays the same: water falls, gravity pulls it downhill, and the flowing water slowly carves a path across the land.
